title: School music programs and Warren Easton High School
summary: Grammar school brought symphony players; Warren Easton had a band and a famed football team, 1937-41.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: No. I don't think you would ever have considered anything but a second class substitute for live music. Live music was the defining thing. And luckily, McDonough 15, the public schools in those days had a good music program. Symphony players would come and demonstrate instruments, you know, in a little grammar school. You know, never do that today. You know, they might put on something and they'd haul 80 busloads of kids to an auditorium somewhere to hear them play or something. Right. And three or four of them would come and show you their instruments and tell you how they made and how they played and why they played that. And that happened in grammar schools in those days.
So you were in, which high school did you go to?
It was a boys' high school then.
Didn't they have a music program? Oh yeah.
Yeah. I know you used to lay them. Big band.

In a lot of ways, it was like a mini LSU, Warren Easton. Same colors, purple and gold, and a big marching band. A great football team. When I went to Warren Easton in 1937 to 1941. I'll explain why in a minute, because if you figure that out, the arithmetic, I was pretty young.

Yeah. But I went to Warren Easton in 1937 to 41. And in 1936, the year before I went to Warren Easton, in the regular season, the football team was undefeated, untied, and unscored on. Of course they went up to Baton Rouge and got beat by a Strumahe, bumped your big farmers, plowed up the field with them. But you know, those were days when Warren Easton had a fantastic athletic program. A very famous guy was the coach, Johnny Brechtel, who was really a good coach. He'd have been a professional coach by today's standards. A really good motivator, smart, and that kind of stuff. And he attracted kids. And then besides that, the public schools had a lot of kids that were very old still in high school. We had a couple guys on the team that were 21 years old, still playing high school football. And they were brutes. In 1937, because I remember this because it was so impressive, the line averaged over 200 pounds. You say, well that's not much, but wait, these were high school kids, okay? And they were huge.
